original_question: How resilient are fixed PQ codebooks to semantic concept drift?
reformulated_question: Can streaming quantization residual statistics detect semantic concept drift and reliably predict ANN Recall@K degradation in Product Quantization before recall drops below an SLA threshold, while controlling for index size growth, codebook aging, and query drift?
problem: In production vector search, exact recall evaluation requires brute-force KNN (O(N*d)), which is too expensive to run continuously on billion-scale indices. Fixed PQ codebooks degrade silently as data distributions shift over time.
existing_knowledge: Static PQ codebooks lose recall when out-of-distribution vectors are inserted (He et al. 2018). Quantization residual magnitude increases as vectors diverge from training centroids.
remaining_uncertainty: Whether inexpensive online residual tracking (O(1) per vector insertion) has sufficient statistical power and lead time to predict downstream Recall@K degradation before SLA violation, and whether it can distinguish genuine semantic drift from innocent index growth.
hypothesis: The cumulative distribution shift of quantization residual norms (measured via Wasserstein distance or exponential moving average of residual error) will exhibit a strong negative correlation (r > 0.85) with Recall@K and provide an early-warning signal at least W batches before recall breaches an SLA threshold (e.g. 90%).
experiment: Feed a chronologically ordered stream of 1.5M ArXiv abstract embeddings (2018-2024) into a fixed PQ/IVF-PQ index. Continuously compute online residual statistics on incoming vectors and periodic Recall@10 on anchor queries. Compare against an I.I.D. insertion control.
dataset_or_workload: Chronologically ordered ArXiv metadata (2018-2024) embedded via Sentence-BERT / BGE-large.
baseline: Static PQ without monitoring; Periodic fixed-interval index rebuilding; Full brute-force ground truth re-indexing.
independent_variables: Drift velocity (temporal stream rate), Quantization granularity (subspace count m, bits b), SLA threshold (e.g. 95%, 90%, 85%).
controlled_variables: Total index vector count (matched against I.I.D. control), Query set distribution (fixed anchor queries vs drifting queries), Hardware environment.
dependent_variables: Early warning lead time (number of vectors before SLA breach), Prediction accuracy (AUC-ROC of SLA violation detection), Computational overhead (latency/memory of residual tracking).
metrics: Recall@10, Mean Quantization Error (MQE), Wasserstein Residual Distance, Lead-time in vector counts, False Positive Alarm Rate.
confounders: Index size expansion (controlled via I.I.D. parallel index), Query distribution shift (isolated via static anchor query test set), Non-uniform cluster popularity.
prior_art: He et al. (TPAMI 2018), Tacnode Technical Report (2024), Liu et al. Rabitq (SIGMOD 2024), VecBench (SIGMOD 2026).
hardware_requirement: Personal desktop or laptop (CPU or single GPU; 8GB-16GB RAM)
main_risk: Residual divergence may correlate with recall drop but offer insufficient lead-time (dropping simultaneously with recall rather than preceding it).

original_question: What is the tail latency penalty of compute/storage decoupling under micro-bursts?
reformulated_question: In compute-storage disaggregated databases under sudden read micro-bursts, does P99 tail latency amplification stem primarily from remote network transport delays or from internal buffer pool latch contention (LWLock:buffer_mapping) during concurrent page fault resolution?
problem: Decoupled serverless databases suffer severe P99 latency spikes during bursty traffic following idle periods. The exact internal bottleneck—network payload fetch versus buffer manager lock serialization—is unclear for systems tuning.
existing_knowledge: Generic cold-fetch latency and cache invalidation under bursty workloads is well-documented in VLDB 2023-2024 (Neon, Gopher, BurScale). Network round-trips to remote storage add significant latency.
remaining_uncertainty: The relative contribution and scaling behavior of internal database concurrency locks (LWLock:buffer_mapping / BufferContent) versus remote network I/O delay as concurrency increases during micro-bursts over Pareto-delayed network links.
hypothesis: Under micro-bursts with >64 concurrent client threads, P99 tail latency is dominated by PostgreSQL buffer pool lock serialization (>60% of total latency) rather than network packet transit time, because concurrent workers serialize on buffer mapping hashes while waiting for pending remote page I/O.
experiment: Deploy a containerized PostgreSQL compute node and a disaggregated storage pageserver connected via a Linux veth pair with tc netem injecting Pareto-distributed network delay (5ms +/- 2ms). Execute micro-burst YCSB read workloads with variable idle windows (10s to 300s) and thread counts (1 to 128), profiling PostgreSQL wait events via pg_stat_activity.
dataset_or_workload: YCSB Workload A/B/C (10M keys) executed via pgbench in burst mode (e.g. 500 queries/sec for 2 seconds, followed by 30 seconds idle).
baseline: Monolithic PostgreSQL with local NVMe; Disaggregated PostgreSQL without network jitter; Single-threaded disaggregated execution.
independent_variables: Burst concurrency (1 to 128 threads), Network injected delay (0ms to 20ms Pareto), Idle period duration (10s to 300s).
controlled_variables: Local buffer pool size (e.g. 25% of working set), Storage engine configuration, CPU core pinning.
dependent_variables: P99 and P99.9 Tail Latency, Wait event distribution (LWLock:buffer_mapping vs IO:DataFileRead), Buffer cache hit ratio.
metrics: Latency percentiles (P50, P95, P99, P99.9), Lock wait time percentage, Throughput (QPS).
confounders: Operating system page cache interference (cleared via drop_caches), TCP connection establishment overhead (persistent connection pool used).
prior_art: Neon VLDB 2023, Gopher VLDB 2024, BurScale ICDE 2024.
main_risk: Prior art in VLDB 2023-2024 already extensively documents disaggregated tail latency, and isolating PostgreSQL lock contention requires non-trivial internal instrumentation.

original_question: Do PTS models exhibit dangerously high false-negative rates on refactoring commits?
reformulated_question: How do specific categories of structural refactorings (class renames, method moves, and cross-module extractions) impact the False Negative Rate of ML-based Predictive Test Selection models across chronologically ordered continuous integration commit streams?
problem: Predictive Test Selection (PTS) uses ML models trained on historical commit diffs and failure correlations to skip tests. When commits perform structural refactorings without changing semantics, file-path and token features decouple from historical test failures, potentially causing silent false negatives (missed regressions).
existing_knowledge: Meta's PTS (Machalica et al. 2019) achieves 99.9% regression recall overall on general commit streams. Refactoring-aware deterministic RTS exists (Silva et al. TOSEM 2023). Industry blogs (BrowserStack 2024) hypothesize that renames/moves cause PTS blind spots, but no empirical academic study has quantified this.
remaining_uncertainty: The exact quantitative failure rate (FNR) of PTS across fine-grained refactoring types; whether structural refactorings exhibit a statistically significantly higher FNR than feature commits; and whether AST-aware or dependency-augmented features can mitigate this blind spot.
hypothesis: Identity-modifying and cross-module refactorings (Rename Class, Move Method across packages) will exhibit a False Negative Rate at least 3x higher than feature commits in standard file-path-based PTS models, because historical file-to-test failure co-occurrence features are broken by path changes.
experiment: Mine continuous chronologically ordered CI commit histories from 15 large open-source Java projects in TravisTorrent / GitHub Actions. Deterministically label every commit using RefactoringMiner 2.0 (pure refactoring, feature, mixed). Train a gradient-boosted decision tree PTS model strictly on historical commits (T1...Ttrain) and evaluate false negatives on future commits (Ttest), stratified by refactoring category.
dataset_or_workload: 15 active open-source Java repositories with extensive CI build logs (from TravisTorrent and GitHub Actions: e.g. commons-lang, jackson-databind, spring-framework, comprising >20,000 sequential CI builds).
baseline: Full Test Suite Execution (Retest-All); Standard File-Path GBDT PTS (Meta ICSE 2019 baseline); Deterministic Dependency RTS (Ekstazi).
independent_variables: Commit Category (Pure Feature vs Pure Refactoring vs Mixed), Refactoring Operation Type (In-file Extract vs Rename Class vs Move Method vs Cross-Module), PTS Feature Representation (File-Path only vs AST/Call-Graph augmented).
controlled_variables: Test selection budget / threshold, Chronological train/val/test temporal boundary (zero future leakage), Project codebases.
dependent_variables: False Negative Rate (percentage of truly failing builds where failing tests were omitted), Test Time Saved, Precision, Recall, AUC-ROC.
metrics: False Negative Rate (FNR), False Omission Rate (FOR), Time Reduction Ratio (TRR), Cohen's d effect size between commit categories.
confounders: Flaky tests (filtered out using re-run logs), Test suite modification in the same commit (controlled by separating test-only modifications), Non-deterministic build failures.
prior_art: Machalica et al. (ICSE-SEIP 2019), Tsantalis et al. (IEEE TSE 2020), Silva et al. (ACM TOSEM 2023), Beller et al. (MSR 2017).
hardware_requirement: Personal laptop or desktop (CPU only; 16GB RAM)
main_risk: The total number of failing builds occurring strictly on pure refactoring commits in open-source projects may be relatively small, requiring mining a large pool of repositories to ensure statistical power.
